title: Astrid and the Alibi
premise: When the coffin of Harrowgate's beloved founder, Edmund Vale, is exhumed for a land dispute and found empty, retired detective Odile Winterbourne is dragged back into investigative work by a desperate young lawyer, Priya Anand, whose client stands accused of murdering Vale twenty years ago. Odile discovers that half the town's founding families have been protecting a secret: Vale faked his death to escape prosecution for fraud, and the one witness who can prove it — his former secretary, presumed dead — has been living in hiding under a new name. As the trial clock ticks down, Odile must choose between exposing the lie that would destroy the town's identity and the truth that would free an innocent man; in the end she finds the witness, trades her testimony for the town's reckoning, and realizes the ragtag circle of allies she's gathered around the bookshop has become the family she never had.
about_author: T. M. Sterling is the pen name of a former small-town journalist who spent a decade covering courthouse trials before turning to fiction. They write mysteries about people rebuilding their lives from the wreckage of old secrets.

chapters.title: The Weight of Empty Paper
chapters.summary: Odile Winterbourne's POV. In her failing bookshop, Odile counts receipts and dodges the bank's calls, haunted by the case that ended her career. When Priya Anand bursts in begging for help on an impossible case, Odile refuses. Emotional beat: exhaustion masking loneliness.

chapters.title: What the Ground Gives Back
chapters.summary: Odile's POV, reluctantly attending the exhumation as Priya's witness. The coffin opens to reveal nothing but river stones and a rotted suit. The crowd gasps; the prosecutor's face goes white. Emotional beat: the old thrill of detection waking like a scar reopening.

chapters.title: Twenty Years of Flowers
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. She interviews the groundskeeper who tended Vale's grave for two decades and notices fresh lilies placed by someone with no official standing. A threatening note appears under her door that night. Emotional beat: unease sharpening into resolve.

chapters.title: The Accused
chapters.summary: Priya's POV. In county jail, Priya meets her client, Danny Ferro, the gardener convicted in absentia of Vale's murder, now facing retrial because of the empty coffin. Danny insists he saw Vale alive after the supposed death date. Emotional beat: desperate hope tempered by fear.

chapters.title: Founders' Row
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. She canvasses the founding families — the Ashcombes, the Merricks, Judge Halloran — and catalogues their identical, rehearsed grief. Each alibi is airtight, which is itself suspicious. Emotional beat: the detective's cold pleasure returning.

chapters.title: Marginalia
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Sorting donated books at the shop, she finds Vale's personal library copy of a local history with handwritten corrections — dates that don't match the official record. Someone has been quietly rewriting the town's story. Emotional beat: curiosity curdling into dread.

chapters.title: The Secretary Who Drowned
chapters.summary: Priya's POV. Digging through probate files, Priya finds that Vale's secretary, Lena Marsh, officially drowned in 2003 — yet her death certificate was filed by the same doctor who signed Vale's. Two convenient deaths, one signature. Emotional beat: triumph shadowed by the scale of the conspiracy.

chapters.title: A Fire at Winterbourne's
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. The bookshop is set ablaze at night; Odile saves the rare books but loses her apartment above the store. The Ashcombe matriarch offers 'charity' — clearly a bribe to walk away. Emotional beat: rage crystallizing into commitment.

chapters.title: Couches and Confessions
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs. Priya takes Odile in; the shop's regulars — teen runaway Felix, widowed postman Gus — rally with casseroles and plywood. Over burnt coffee, Odile admits why she left the force. Emotional beat: the found family assembling without anyone naming it.

chapters.title: The Doctor's Ledger
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. She tracks down the doctor's widow and finds his hidden ledger: payments from Vale himself, dated after his death. Vale was alive, paying for silence — until the payments stopped. Emotional beat: vindication tangled with pity.

chapters.title: What Danny Saw
chapters.summary: Danny's POV (via deposition). Danny recounts the night he saw Vale alive at the boathouse, arguing with someone whose face he never saw — and how he was framed for a murder that never happened. Emotional beat: an innocent man's quiet dignity breaking the reader's heart.

chapters.title: Judge Halloran's Debt
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Odile confronts Judge Halloran, who confesses Vale blackmailed him over an old scandal; he signed the death paperwork to make the fraud permanent. He won't testify — duty to the town outweighs truth. Emotional beat: love versus duty embodied in a broken man.

chapters.title: Lilies in the Fog
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Following the lily deliveries, Odile stakes out the cemetery at dawn and glimpses a woman in a gray coat leaving flowers — then losing her in the fog. But she drops a pharmacy receipt with a partial name. Emotional beat: hope running on adrenaline.

chapters.title: The Trial Begins
chapters.summary: Priya's POV. Opening arguments; the prosecution pivots to claim Danny moved the body. Priya's evidence of the fake death is ruled inadmissible without a living witness. The clock becomes literal: find Lena Marsh or lose. Emotional beat: the walls closing in.

chapters.title: Ashcomb House
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Breaking into the Ashcombe estate, Odile finds correspondence proving the families funded Vale's disappearance to protect their fortunes — and a photograph of Lena Marsh alive, taken five years ago. Emotional beat: betrayal layered on betrayal.

chapters.title: The Woman in Gray
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Using the receipt and the photograph, Odile traces Lena to a coastal cottage two towns over. Their confrontation is raw: Lena watched an innocent man rot rather than testify against the man she loved. Emotional beat: loyalty versus truth made flesh.

chapters.title: Ninety-Six Hours
chapters.summary: Ensemble POV. With three days until closing arguments, Lena wavers; the Ashcombes escalate, threatening Felix's custody status and Priya's bar license. The bookshop family closes ranks around Odile. Emotional beat: fear answered by solidarity.

chapters.title: The Boathouse Reckoning
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Odile reconstructs the real crime: when Vale tried to return and reclaim his fortune, the Ashcombe patriarch killed him in earnest and used the empty coffin to bury the secret forever. She finds Vale's true remains where Danny's sighting places them. Emotional beat: horror and clarity arriving together.

chapters.title: Testimony
chapters.summary: Courtroom, alternating Odile and Priya POVs. Lena takes the stand; Halloran, shamed by her courage, recants and corroborates. The physical evidence seals it. Danny walks free. Emotional beat: catharsis — truth finally outranking loyalty.

chapters.title: What the Town Owes
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. The fallout: indictments, the founder's statue coming down, neighbors who won't meet Odile's eye — and others who leave thank-you notes in the shop's return slot. Emotional beat: the cost of truth counted honestly.

chapters.title: Reopening
chapters.summary: Ensemble POV. The community rebuilds the bookshop together; Felix gets a job, Gus installs shelves, Priya brings champagne. Odile hangs a new sign: open. Emotional beat: warmth earned, not given.

chapters.title: Astrid
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Odile adopts the stray cat that sheltered in the burned shop through the fire — Astrid — and writes the first page of her memoir. The last line: some families you're born into; others you detect. Emotional beat: peace, and the promise of more cases.
